memory_leads.lead: A liner service string is a recurring round-voyage design that links a vessel set, ordered port rotation and target frequency; network capacity therefore depends on maintaining the cycle, not merely owning ships.

Port rotation and call sequencing allocate scarce voyage time across origin/destination markets; adding, omitting or resequencing calls changes transit time, connection quality and the number of ships needed to preserve frequency.
Vessel deployment matches ship size, speed, draft/port capability and expected cargo mix to a service; the same vessel can create different network capacity depending on where it is deployed.

Alliance/VSA-style networks can separate vessel operation from commercial slot access: one carrier may sell space on a sailing operated by another, so operator, service participation and customer-facing capacity are distinct states.

Slot exchange, slot purchase or slot-charter style arrangements can rebalance capacity between partners or services without transferring vessel ownership; exact agreement structures and economics are deferred.

Transshipment creates a connection-dependent network layer in which one container itinerary spans multiple sailings; missed connections or hub congestion can break service even when each individual vessel has capacity.

Feeder services connect smaller regional ports to mainline hubs and can be operated by the same carrier, partners or common feeders; feeder timing and capacity therefore become part of end-to-end liner reliability.
Berth windows and planned terminal call windows couple the ocean schedule to terminal resources; a late ship can lose its intended window and experience additional delay or operational resequencing.

Blank sailings or cancelled voyages can deliberately remove near-term marketed capacity, sometimes for demand management and sometimes for schedule recovery; the operational reason matters more than treating every blank as identical supply withdrawal.

Extra loaders or ad-hoc additional sailings can temporarily add capacity or evacuate backlog outside the regular service pattern, creating a short-lived supply response distinct from permanent network deployment.
Cascading redeploys vessels across trades as larger/newer ships enter core routes, transmitting capacity changes between markets even when total fleet size changes slowly.

Schedule disruption can create vessel bunching: multiple late ships arrive close together after gaps, producing highly uneven effective weekly capacity, terminal peaks and customer service despite unchanged monthly nominal slots.

Recovery actions include port omissions, speed changes, rotation truncation, inducement/additional calls, connection protection or voyage resets; schedule reliability is therefore an actively managed state rather than only a measured outcome.

Effective liner capacity should include network position and timing: a TEU slot arriving on the wrong week, wrong service or after a missed transshipment is not equivalent to an on-time usable slot for the booked cargo.

Alliance scale can improve network breadth and asset utilization while increasing coordination and connection dependencies; structural capacity sharing is not identical to operational schedule resilience.

Chokepoint rerouting or longer voyage distance can require additional vessels to maintain a weekly service or force lower frequency/port omissions, connecting tonne-mile shocks directly to liner schedule capacity.

Schedule reliability propagates into P017/P018 states: late or bunched services disturb empty-equipment repositioning, transshipment connections, booking rollovers and allocation fulfillment even before fleet supply changes.

The broad facts that liner networks use alliances/VSA structures and that blank sailings can absorb effective capacity are already present in the atlas; P019 retains only their network-state mechanics.
The general point that routing distance and chokepoints alter effective capacity is already established; P019 only refines how the effect enters a recurring liner service cycle.

stop_reason: The liner-network layer is populated from service design and vessel deployment through slot sharing, transshipment/feeder connections, blank/extra capacity and schedule recovery; further recall becomes carrier-, alliance-, lane-, timetable- or agreement-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no carrier schedule, alliance agreement, slot quantity, blank-sailing event, reliability metric or historical network deployment is verified.
